questions.stem: An 82-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of fever and confusion. He had a history of atrial fibrillation, CABG 4 years ago, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He was a resident in a nursing home and had a long-term catheter in situ. He had been treated presumptively for a urinary tract infection but had deteriorated. On examination his GCS was 13/15, his temperature was 38.1°C, and his heart rate was 112 beats/minute. His blood pressure was 128/68 mmHg. It was not possible to formally examine his neurologic systems, but his reflexes were universally brisk and his tone increased. There were no lateralizing signs. Pupils were equal and reactive to light. He was admitted and treated with antibiotics for presumed urosepsis. Two days after his admission, he had a tonic clonic seizure on the ward. An urgent MRI showed temporal lobe enhancement, and a lumbar puncture showed a lymphocytic CSF with a raised red cell count. CSF PCR was positive for HSV-1. Six months after discharge he was still suffering from significant cognitive impairment with behavioral abnormalities.
questions.lead_in: What factor in this case is associated with a poor outcome?

options.text: MRI changes in the temporal lobes

questions.explanation: Delay in initiating aciclovir therapy Herpes encephalitis carries a high morbidity and mortality even with prompt diagnosis and appropriate treatment. A multivariate analysis identified two factors associated with a poorer outcome. These were a high “simplified acute physiology score” at admission and a delay of longer than 2 days between admission and starting aciclovir therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q11

questions.question: A young post-appendectomy patient with an indwelling Foley catheter has cloudy, foul-smelling urine but is otherwise asymptomatic. Urine culture grows Escherichia coli and an antibiogram is provided. What is the management?
questions.question_raw: Young patient with long vignette of asymptomatic bacteriuria on post appendectomy? Foley cath. His urine is cloudy and nauseating. A culture is positive for E. coli and the antibiogram is given. What is the management?
questions.model_answer: This is catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB), not CAUTI: he has no urinary or systemic signs, and cloudy or malodorous urine in a catheterized patient has no demonstrated clinical significance. (1) Do NOT give antibiotics regardless of the antibiogram — screening for and treating ASB in short-term catheterized patients is not recommended (exceptions are pregnancy and traumatic genitourinary procedures with mucosal bleeding), and unnecessary treatment drives resistance and C. difficile. (2) Assess whether the catheter is still needed and remove it as soon as possible; if it must stay and has been in for a while, replace it. (3) Monitor clinically for genuine symptoms/signs of CAUTI (new fever, flank/CVA pain, rigors, altered mental status) and treat only if these develop.

cohort_answer.text: No treatment. Change foley cath. Monitor clinically

questions.question: A hospitalized woman with an indwelling Foley catheter, post-appendectomy, has cloudy foul-smelling urine, temperature 37.2°C, WBC 12, and is otherwise asymptomatic. Urine culture grows a susceptible organism and urinalysis shows some leukocytes. What would you do?
questions.question_raw: A woman in hospital with cloudy foul smelling urine with indwelling foley. T 37.2C, WBC 12, post-op appendectomy. Otherwise no symptoms. Growing something that's pretty sensitive in Ucx, some leuks on UA.
questions.model_answer: This is catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria: she is afebrile with no urinary symptoms, and cloudy/foul urine and pyuria are nonspecific in a catheterized patient. (1) Do NOT prescribe antibiotics — screening for and treating ASB in short-term (<30 day) catheterized patients is not recommended and only selects for resistance. (2) Remove the Foley if it is no longer required (short-term post-op catheter). (3) Monitor clinically and treat only if true CAUTI signs/symptoms not explained by another cause emerge.

cohort_answer.text: Remove Foley. No abx indicated. IDSA: in patients with short-term indwelling urethral catheter (<30 days), recommend against screening for or treating asymptomatic bacteriuria (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence)

questions.question: You are seeing a patient with a catheter-associated urinary tract infection.
questions.question_raw: You are seeing a patient with a catheter-associated UTI.

parts.text: What is the MOST important factor associated with catheter-associated urinary tract infection?
What THREE options could be used instead of an indwelling urethral catheter in a patient requiring a catheter?
In a male patient with uncomplicated febrile catheter-associated UTI, what would be the typical treatment duration?

parts_raw.text: What factor is the MOST important factor associated with catheter associated UTI?
What THREE options could be used instead of an indwelling urethral catheter in a patient requiring a catheter?
In a male patient with uncomplicated febrile catheter associated UTI, what would be the typical treatment duration?

questions.model_answer:
a) Duration of catheterization — it is the single most important risk factor for the development of catheter-associated bacteriuria/CAUTI.
b) (1) External (condom) catheter. (2) Intermittent (in-and-out) catheterization. (3) Suprapubic catheterization.
c) Approximately 7 days. A 7-day course is reasonable for most patients with CAUTI who respond promptly; shorter (5-day fluoroquinolone) courses suffice in milder cases and longer (up to 10–14 days) courses are used for slow responders or complications.
